offence_severity: imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and shall also be liable to fine
number_of_offences: Number of offences/counts charged: 2; finally upheld: 1
key_evidence_accepted: Evidence of the prosecution witnesses and the circumstantial evidence makes it amply clear that deceased was subjected to cruelty at the hands of her husband and her in-laws which had caused her grave mental and physical injury.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as credible, noting that their testimony was corroborated by other independent witnesses and that the veracity of their testimony was tested on objective parameters.
post_offence_conduct: The accused were present inside the house at the time the deceased consumed the poisonous tablet and took her to the hospital as soon as they realized she was in a critical condition.
trial_duration: Dates of offence not specified; trial judgment dated 21.11.2009; High Court decision dated 23.02.2015; Supreme Court decision dated 14.09.2015
legal_representation: Santosh Krishnan, Nikhil Goel, Naveen Goel, Marsook Bafaki for the Appellants; Hemantika Wahi, Jesal Wahi, Puja Singh for the Respondent
investigation_status: FIR registered; charge sheet filed; trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction and sentence passed; High Court: Dismissed appeal, upheld conviction and sentence; Supreme Court: Partly allowed the appeal, set aside conviction under Section 306
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the deceased was subjected to cruelty by her husband and in-laws, which led her to commit suicide. The accused were convicted under Sections 498A and 306 of the Indian Penal Code.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the prosecution failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the accused had abetted the deceased in committing suicide. They emphasized the deceased's dying declaration stating she consumed poison by mistake and the accused's actions in taking her to the hospital.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt that the accused abetted the deceased's suicide, and that the deceased's dying declaration and conduct of the accused were critical in this determination.
precedent_relied_upon: Vishwanath Agrawal v. Sar/a Vishwanath Agrawal (2012) 7 SCC 288; Bhola Turha v. State of Bihar (1998) 9 SCC 15; Ramesh Kumar v. State of Chhattisgarh (2001) 9 SCC 618
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed considering the age of the appellants and their responsibility for caring for a child, limiting the sentence to the period already undergone by them.
judicial_mitigating_factors: The age of the appellants and their responsibility for caring for a child.
other_sentence_order: The appellants were directed to be released from custody as the sentence was modified to the period already undergone.
